titre: The 27th U.S. Amendment: Proposed in 1789, Ratified in 1992
accroche: An amendment sent to the states in 1789 did not enter the U.S. Constitution until 1992, after a college paper graded C.
contenu_vulgarise:
On September 25, 1789, the U.S. Congress sends the states twelve proposed amendments to the Constitution. Ten will become the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791. Another is forgotten: it says that no law changing the pay of senators and representatives may take effect until an election of the House of Representatives has taken place. Lawmakers therefore cannot vote themselves a raise they would enjoy right away.

## A text that went nowhere

By the end of 1791, six of the fourteen existing states have ratified the text. It needed eleven, at least three-fourths. The amendment stays in limbo, with no one declaring it dead. In 1873, Ohio ratifies it to protest a pay raise Congress has just granted itself; in 1978, Wyoming does the same against a raise granted in 1977. These are isolated gestures of anger: the Congressional Research Service notes that the amendment then lies dormant until the end of the 20th century.

## A paper, then a campaign

In 1982, Gregory Watson, an undergraduate at the University of Texas at Austin, picks this forgotten text for a paper. His thesis is that Congress set no deadline for ratification, so the text can still be adopted. His grade is a C. Watson does not let it go: he runs a letter-writing campaign aimed at state legislatures. Maine ratifies on April 27, 1983, the first state to do so following this campaign, then Colorado on April 22, 1984. From the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, more than thirty state legislatures follow.

On May 18, 1992, the Archivist of the United States, Don W. Wilson, certifies the amendment as ratified, effective May 7, 1992. The House and the Senate then each adopt a resolution acknowledging the fact, although the Constitution does not require this confirmation. More than two centuries have passed between the vote in Congress and the amendment's entry into the Constitution.

## What this changes

We readily assume that a proposed amendment expires with its era: one generation rejects it, the next stops thinking about it. This case shows the opposite. Here, according to Watson's argument, Congress had written no deadline into the proposal, and the Archivist certified the ratification in 1992: the ratifications added up over more than two centuries without time counting against them.

The question this story leaves open is one of consent: what is the agreement of six legislatures in 1791 and of more than thirty others in the late 20th century worth, when the states, the country, and the Congress that was meant to hear their voice have nothing left in common with those of 1789?

repere.texte: On September 25, 1789, Congress submits to the states a proposed amendment on the pay of members of Congress. By the end of 1791, 6 of 14 states have ratified it; 11 were needed. The Archivist of the United States certifies it as ratified on May 18, 1992, effective May 7, 1992.
repere.source: Congressional Research Service, The Twenty-Seventh Amendment and Congressional Compensation, March 14, 2023

carte.punch: Proposed in 1789, ratified in 1992: an amendment took two centuries to take effect.
carte.idee: In 1789, the U.S. Congress submits to the states a text on its members' pay. Only six states ratify it before the end of 1791. In 1982, a Texas student revives the idea in a paper graded C, then with the legislatures: the Archivist certifies it as ratified in 1992.

quiz.question: Why could an amendment sent to the states in 1789 be ratified in 1992?
choix: Congress had passed a special law in 1992 to reopen ratification
No ratification deadline had been set in the 1789 proposal
The 1791 ratifications had been enough, and 1992 merely recorded an old vote
The Archivist has the power to add an amendment when he sees fit
quiz.explication: Congress had set no time limit for ratification: that is Watson's argument, and the Archivist certified the amendment as ratified. The 1791 ratifications were not enough (6 of 14 states, 11 required); Congress did not pass a law to reopen the process, its two chambers merely acknowledged the amendment through resolutions, and the Archivist does not create amendments: he certifies a result.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does the text of the 27th Amendment, proposed in 1789, say?
choix: That no law changing the pay of members of Congress takes effect before a House election
That senators may not serve more than two consecutive terms
That Congress must pass its own budget every year before October 1
That any congressional pay raise must be approved by referendum
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The 1789 text, reported by the National Archives and the CRS, forbids a law changing the pay of members of Congress from taking effect until a House election has intervened. Nothing in it concerns terms, the budget, or a referendum.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Which state is the first to ratify the amendment following Gregory Watson's letter-writing campaign?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to English Wikipedia (a chronology drawn from the CRS), Maine ratifies on April 27, 1983, the first state to do so after Watson's letter campaign; Colorado follows in 1984. Ohio (1873) and Wyoming (1978) had ratified earlier, as isolated protests.
